source.title: Feature learning and generalization in deep networks with orthogonal weights
source.authors: Hannah Day; Yonatan Kahn; Daniel A. Roberts

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares orthogonal and Gaussian initializations in full-batch gradient descent and reports training-loss behavior, but does not measure the training classification error specified by V1.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from its own training experiments. Its initialization, depth, optimizer, and loss-function variations bear on V4. Training-loss and validation-loss results do not directly measure V1's training classification error. Values available only in figures are recorded as figure only. Results cited from earlier studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares equal-variance orthogonal and Gaussian initialization using learning curves in plain tanh MLPs, testing V4's training-speed prediction. It also varies initialization variance to test the importance of avoiding vanishing or exploding gradients. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors report consistent but modest orthogonal-initialization benefits in critical deep tanh networks: percent-level test-loss improvements and order-one improvements in training epochs. Suppressed NTK-related fluctuations are a proposed explanation, supported empirically rather than fully derived. Advantages are negligible in shallow regimes, mild or uncertain for ReLU, and do not eliminate failures from noncritical variance. They explicitly question the practical benefit because the best-performing tested architectures are shallow.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses orthogonal initialization and full-batch gradient descent, as relevant to V4, but tests fully connected tanh or ReLU MLPs on MNIST and CIFAR-10 rather than the listed plain tanh network and convolutional initialization settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary with depth-to-width regime, activation, criticality of initialization, optimizer, and loss. Orthogonal and Gaussian results are nearly identical for L/n ≪ 1; advantages are clearer for deep tanh networks with L/n ≃ 1. ReLU yields at most a mild training-speed advantage. Noncritical CW = 0.1 or CW = 10 leads to vanishing-gradient or divergence problems for both initializations.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonal initialization gives somewhat lower best test loss; the best tested hidden depths are 3 for MNIST and 4 for CIFAR-10 under both initializations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization affects generalization, while the depth minimizing held-out loss can remain the same across initializations.

record.problems: The experiments use toy MLPs and datasets, with 10 runs for MNIST and 5 for CIFAR-10; some training-dynamics illustrations use a single instantiation. Main reported performance measures are validation or test losses, not training classification error. NTK correlator recursion derivations for orthogonal weights are left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every plotted depth in Figures 4–7: the paper's text summarizes those depth ranges collectively, and the plotted values are figure only. No rows for cited prior-study results, initialization correlator measurements, or NTK-only measurements that do not directly measure training speed or training outcome.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including CIFAR-100 and corrupted or random labels; effects of model size, early stopping and regularized recipes on that error.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks versus identity-shortcut networks; special very-deep plain-tanh and normalization-free residual recipes.

Orthogonal convolution kernels and training 10,000-layer plain CNNs; maximal trainable depth; broader activation-matched initialization recipes and architectures beyond the tested MLPs. Validation/test loss minima do not establish maximal trainable depth.

Learning rates relative to initial linearized stability thresholds, curvature or sharpness evolution, catapult recovery and divergence relative to those thresholds. Loss oscillations alone do not establish these effects.
Batch-normalization speed and learning-rate comparisons, and Fixup residual networks.

missing.what: At hidden depth 5 and CW = 10, Gaussian initialization diverges in approximately one quarter of runs, whereas orthogonal initialization has zero divergences in 20 attempted runs. This shallow stability difference contrasts with the similar depth-30 failure rates already recorded.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figure 16 caption and accompanying discussion

missing.what: Separate matched shallow-network comparisons: ordinary GD, Adam and cross-entropy yield nearly identical performance for orthogonal and Gaussian initialization at hidden depth 5. Existing depth-30 rows should not contain these additional conditions.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figures 18–20 and accompanying discussion

record.verdict_notes: ReLU's weak orthogonal advantage does not challenge V4's tanh-specific comparison. Noncritical failures support the stated signal-propagation condition rather than imposing an additional limitation. Generalization loss and NTK fluctuations are not substitutes for training-speed measurements. The record's declared omissions already cover initialization-correlator measurements and collective plotted-depth results.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, zero or near-zero error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and extra student width.
Plain convolutional networks versus identity shortcuts, and normalization in residual networks.

Activation-matched initializations beyond the paper's tanh and ReLU experiments; training plain tanh networks at 10,000 layers; orthogonal convolution kernels; and comparisons of orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization at equal variance for other activations and architectures.
Learning rates above the stability threshold, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence as a function of the stability limit.
Batch normalization comparisons and Fixup residual networks.
